name: mat2
why: Stripping metadata means looking hard at file internals, and seeing what hides in your own files is a genuine eye-opener.

brief.what_it_is: mat2 is a metadata anonymization toolkit that strips hidden metadata from files such as images, PDFs, Office documents, audio, video, archives and SVGs. It ships as a Python library called libmat2, a command line tool called mat2, and a service menu for the Dolphin file manager. You give it files; it writes cleaned copies alongside the originals, and with --show it lists the metadata it can detect without removing it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says files carry metadata that can reveal who made them and when: cameras record when and with what a picture was taken, and Office and PDF tools add author and company information. The stated job is 'getting rid, as much as possible, of metadata.'
brief.how_it_works: mat2 dispatches each file to a format-specific cleaner, relying on helpers such as ExifTool, FFmpeg, mutagen and GObject-introspection bindings for Poppler, GdkPixbuf and librsvg, depending on the format. By default it may re-encode or alter content to strip more metadata. The -L (lightweight) flag removes only some metadata and promises not to modify the file's data.

brief.install_notes: The README requires python3.11 or newer. Debian-style packages named in the requirements list are python3-mutagen (audio), python3-gi-cairo and gir1.2-poppler-0.18 (PDF), gir1.2-gdkpixbuf-2.0 (images), gir1.2-rsvg-2.0 (SVG), FFmpeg (optional, video), and libimage-exiftool-perl (everything else). The stated baseline is current Debian oldstable, or Debian stable if oldstable is end-of-life. The README gives a macOS Homebrew line, but no PyPI or Homebrew-specific install steps beyond that. Nothing is said about accounts or first-run configuration.
brief.standout: mat2 is candid that it cannot prove a file is clean: the README says there is no reliable way to detect every possible metadata field, so an empty --show result should not be trusted. It also offers an explicit trade-off between thorough stripping, which may alter content (for example, PDF text may stop being selectable), and a lightweight mode that leaves the data alone.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog or last-commit information, and I did not fetch the releases or commits pages. It is an active-looking project: it targets python3.11 and recent formats such as AVIF and JPEG XL, and it links a companion web service and a GTK GUI. Those are inferences, not confirmed activity.
brief.caveats: Cleaning is best effort; the README warns that detection and removal are not guaranteed complete. The default mode can change the content of files, and -L trades some metadata removal for data preservation. mat2 never cleans in place; it writes a .cleaned copy, and --inplace is the only way to overwrite, without backup. The --unknown-members flag defaults to abort for archive-style files. Several dependencies are needed for full format coverage, and the README gives package lists only for Debian and Homebrew. The README's license section mixes LGPL-3.0 wording in the header with GPL text in the body, so check the LICENSE file before relying on it. The homepage is a GitHub repository, and I read the README directly, so no install from source was tested.
quotes: Keep your data, trash your meta!

mat2 **will not** clean files in-place, but will produce, for example, with a file named "myfile.png" a cleaned version named "myfile.cleaned.png".
